column2: * * * Xiaogouzi proved most eager to oblige. The noon gun had scarcely sounded when he arrived with his party, five men in all. Three remained in the courtyard with sacks and carrying poles; the one he brought indoors was, plainly, A’qiao's husband. Said to be surnamed Chen, he was about forty, a timid, thoroughly honest-looking fellow. Over a bulky padded jacket he wore a brand-new blue cotton gown, with straw sandals on his bare feet. Once inside, he shrank against the doorway, looking either embarrassed or frightened. “Sit down, please.” Hu turned to Xiaogouzi. “Everything agreed?” “Everything.” He took out two written agreements on mulberry-bark paper. Even the letter of divorce was ready. Hu read them through. They were drawn up very securely, and he expressed his satisfaction. “This will do.” Pointing to Zhou Yiming, he said, “Here's the intermediary for our side. You represent the other side. We still need a scribe. Let the bookkeeper at Jinchang Inn earn a little.” “Mr Hu,” Xiaogouzi hastened to interrupt, “we've brought our own scribe.” He called outside, “Mr Liu!” Of the five men, this Mr Liu alone wore a long gown. His furtive, ratlike appearance suggested no good character.

Hu suddenly grew suspicious. Then he realized that he had forgotten an indispensable move. Keeping up appearances, he drew Zhou aside and whispered, “I've overlooked something. Does this Chen fellow look like A’qiao's husband to you?” “How could anyone tell by looking?” “Suppose he's an impostor? The money would be a small matter; we'd make fools of ourselves. Yesterday I forgot to tell them to bring their clan head.” “That can still be done. I'll speak to Xiaogouzi.” “Going back and forth would waste time and cause trouble. So long as we establish his identity and know he isn't an impostor, it doesn't matter whether the Chen clan head comes.” “Who can tell whether he's an impostor?” Zhou said. “Unless we ask A’qiao herself to identify him.” That went straight to the heart of it. There was no better way. Hu considered, then resolved on a delaying manoeuvre. Zhou was told to take Xiaogouzi to lunch, while Hu left Jinchang Inn on the pretext of going to a bank to obtain silver, and took a sedan chair straight to the Pans' house.

With a visiting card and a generous gratuity for the doorkeeper, Hu frankly explained his purpose. Whether the master received him did not matter; he had come to see A’qiao. Pan Shuya was a young master who dreaded worldly social obligations. On hearing the doorkeeper's report, he was glad of the excuse to spare himself the trouble and asked A’qiao to go out directly. Seeing Hu arrive empty-handed, she was disappointed and could not help complaining. “You ought to help me make a proper return. They're so kind to me here that I really feel uneasy.” “Don't worry. I've already made plans. You'll certainly have every reason to hold your head high. But there's no time for that now. Come back to the inn at once and identify someone.” “Identify someone? Who?” She blinked her exceptionally long lashes, thoroughly puzzled. “Think. Who else could there be that only you could identify?” The question made his meaning plain, yet she was more bewildered than ever. “What exactly has happened?” She was displeased that he should handle so important a matter without consulting her. “Unless you explain, I won't go,” she said firmly. Hu quickly took the hint and smiled apologetically. “Don't blame me for acting on my own. First, I had no chance to tell you; second, I wanted to spare you worry. I meant well.” “Thank you for your good intentions.” She accepted his explanation, though some resentment remained. She also found her position awkward. “Face to face, like a gong answering a drum—how am I supposed to identify him?” “No, no. You needn't face him. Just look through a crack in the partition. Once you've identified him, there's nothing more for you to do.” He briefly explained how he had brought Xiaogouzi round.

“You have so many tricks!” A’qiao said with a smile. Then her face suddenly grew serious. She looked down at the brick floor and remained silent for a long time. Hu became anxious and began to regret his lack of care. That she and her husband were on bad terms was something he had heard only from Second Miss at Yiqing House. Her own conduct did suggest that she had almost severed relations with her husband's family, but much of what people in such establishments said was unreliable. As the saying went, they could deceive a man to death without paying with their lives. He had taken it all for truth and set about the matter in earnest; at the critical moment, he might merely bring trouble upon himself. A’qiao might not have meant to deceive him. Still, every household had its own difficult scripture to recite. She evidently had some private concern that deserved understanding. In the end, he had been rash and could not blame her. Whether to blame her was secondary, however. If she refused her consent now, how was he to explain matters to Xiaogouzi? To come to Suzhou on such an absurd errand and become a laughingstock was more loss of face than he could bear. He urgently needed a truthful answer. “Sister A’qiao,” he said gravely, “you can't put me off any longer. Tell me honestly what you really want.” “Why!” She was astonished. “When have I ever lied to put you off?” “Then why do you seem ready to beat a retreat, now that things have come this far?” She found this amusing. “I've never sat in court like a county magistrate. How can I beat the drum that closes the hearing?”

Her words sounded more troublesome still. On closer examination, there was a barb in them. Before undertaking the matter, Hu had neither told her nor obtained her consent: she had never ‘opened court’, so how could she now beat the drum to close it? She was a formidable woman. This was no time to reason with her, since the right was not on his side and he could not win the argument. He could only appeal to her feelings, even deceive her a little if necessary. First, he admitted his fault. “I've handled this badly. But I'll certainly follow your wishes and won't force you. The man is there now. Come and identify him first, and we'll decide afterwards. If he's the wrong man, there's nothing more to discuss. If he's the right one, it's entirely up to you. Whichever way you wish to go, I won't object.” After all, a human heart was made of flesh. Hearing this, A’qiao could hesitate no longer. In fact, she was not reluctant because of lingering affection for her husband. She was thinking of her own family: Hu ought to provide some money to support her mother in old age. This condition seemed best discussed along with the other arrangements, but she did not know how to raise it. That was the cause of her hesitation; Hu had misunderstood. “Then sit down a moment. I must tell my hosts.” She added, “Did you hire a chair?” “Easily arranged. I'll leave mine for you and hire another. When you reach Jinchang Inn, come through the side entrance. I'll have someone waiting.”

With this settled, Hu left first. He had twice used these chair-bearers from near Chang Gate and knew them already. After giving his instructions, he hired another chair and hurried back to Jinchang Inn. There he rented an additional room and told an attendant to wait expressly at the side entrance. When A’qiao arrived, he was to bring her in quietly, then show himself to Hu without speaking. Only after everything was arranged did Hu return to his own room. Before long, Zhou brought Xiaogouzi and the others back from lunch. All their faces were red; they seemed to have drunk a good deal. After further courtesies, Hu launched into a wide-ranging account of Suzhou's scenery. Zhou understood that he meant to gain time and joined in. The conversation was lively, but never touched their business. Xiaogouzi could hardly bear it. At last, finding an opening, he interjected, “Mr Hu, we still want to get back to Mudu today. It'll be inconvenient if we're too late. Shall we begin?” “Oh, yes. Forgive me,” Hu replied apologetically. “Just a little longer. As soon as the bank's man comes and we have the full amount of silver, we'll begin. It's only a matter of putting down a mark. It won't take long.” Xiaogouzi had to wait patiently again, though his uneasiness became increasingly apparent. Watching coolly, Hu grew more suspicious and secretly devised a second plan. He was about to find an excuse to consult Zhou privately when the attendant appeared. Showing presence of mind, the man came with a pot to replenish the tea and gave Hu a covert glance. Even Zhou failed to notice.

Hu excused himself and went to see A’qiao in another part of the inn. “In a moment I'll bring someone out. Look carefully, but don't speak. I'll come back shortly.” Returning to the others, he beckoned to the supposed husband. The shrinking middle-aged man merely looked at Xiaogouzi, seeking guidance with his eyes. “Mr Hu, whatever you want to say, say it to me.” “Nothing important. But it isn't something for outsiders to hear.” Hu beckoned repeatedly. “Come here, please.” A countryman might be unused to polite society, but why be so reluctant to exchange a few private words? Xiaogouzi could hardly obstruct him further. Chen had no choice but to steel himself and follow his host outside. Hu was no ordinary man. Seeing Chen as wooden as a puppet, with Xiaogouzi pulling the strings, he had already guessed most of the truth without waiting for A’qiao's identification. He led him out to face the window behind which she was concealed. His first question was, “What is your actual surname?” “Chen.” The answer came readily enough to be true. Hu asked his second question. “What relation are you to A’qiao?” This exposed him. He stammered and muttered incoherently. Just as I thought! Hu silently reproached himself. Without that last-minute inspiration, Xiaogouzi would have cheated him of more than a thousand taels. He would have capsized in an open ditch—a humiliation he could not even complain of, since publicizing it would give people an irresistible story against him.

Inwardly both angry and amused, Hu kept his expression and voice unchanged. Instead, he offered reassurance. “Old Chen, I know all about Xiaogouzi's trick. Tell me the truth and I won't make trouble for you. I won't expose you to him afterwards either, so you needn't be put in a difficult position.” This last assurance touched the honest fellow where it mattered. “Mr Hu, if I tell you the truth,” he asked earnestly, “you really won't tell Xiaogouzi?” “Really. Do you want me to swear an oath?” Reassured, Chen revealed everything. He was an elder cousin of A’qiao's husband. He owed Xiaogouzi money and had been forced to submit to him and impersonate her husband. The agreement was that his old debt would be cancelled and he would receive a large silver ingot besides. What an absurd affair! “Aren't you afraid of being taken to court?” Hu asked. “I am,” Chen answered miserably. “But Xiaogouzi says there's nothing to fear. The intermediary and the scribe are all our own people. If a complaint reaches the county yamen, we'll just say the document is false and nothing of the sort happened.” The scoundrel! Hu thought. Xiaogouzi was a shrewd one and deserved a lesson. He whispered, “Don't be afraid. Whatever he tells you to do afterwards, do it. Just insist that you haven't told me the truth, and he won't blame you.” A simple-minded man needed instructions of this sort. Chen understood and nodded repeatedly. “I know. I know.”

They went back inside one after the other. Xiaogouzi's expression shifted uncertainly, but relaxed at once when Hu spoke. “Come, let's begin. Draw up the documents, then take your silver and get back to Mudu early. That will save everyone trouble.” Zhou knew nothing of what had happened. He assumed that Chen's identity as A’qiao's husband had been confirmed, a satisfactory conclusion. Cheerfully, he set out brush and inkstone and had Xiaogouzi spread the documents on the table. Zhou first signed his mark as intermediary. Xiaogouzi and the scribe followed, each taking the brush to draw a cross. Last came Chen, who could not even draw a cross and had to make an inked handprint. With the formalities complete, it was time to hand over the payment. Hu said, “Old Zhou, you're the intermediary. Hold the documents for now, and give them to me after the money has been paid in full.” He gave a slight signal with his eyes. Zhou understood at once: there was another move to come! He snatched up the papers, folded them in half and then in quarters, and gripped them firmly.

Hu continued, “Marriage is a serious matter. Whether people unite or separate, everything must be clear. The documents are drawn up, but only one of the two parties is present. Even the man is someone we've just met.” He turned to Zhou. “As intermediary, what would you say if a dispute arose later?” Knowing the question was deliberate, Zhou pretended surprise. “What dispute could there be?” “Exactly!” Xiaogouzi hastened to add. “There can't possibly be any dispute.” “Not so.” Hu pointed at Chen. “He doesn't much resemble A’qiao's husband to me. I asked him privately just now, and he insisted he was. Leave that aside. These documents still need one formality before they can be accepted. When we conduct affairs for others, we must make everything secure. If trouble arises when either party remarries, it will be a serious matter.” “Quite right,” Zhou put in. “It's no easy thing to act as intermediary. If this were merely a dispute about a debt, at worst I could repay the money. But if we've mistaken the person, how could I provide another A’qiao in compensation?” “Precisely,” Hu said. “Whether he's the genuine man or an impostor, we can't settle without A’qiao here to identify him, so let's leave that aside too. At least we must be able to prove that the documents are genuine.” Hearing that A’qiao was absent, Xiaogouzi felt greatly relieved. His mind grew more agile. “You're quite right, Mr Hu. That's exactly why we have intermediaries and a scribe—to prove the papers genuine. I don't understand what further witness you want.” Hu smiled faintly. “We have them, certainly. But let's speak plainly. If a dispute went to court, the magistrate couldn't rely on Old Zhou's testimony alone. Why don't we register the documents at the county yamen's revenue office and have them stamped with an official seal, like the red deeds used for buying land? I'll pay all the expenses.” Zhou was first to approve. “Excellent! That will lessen our responsibility as intermediaries,” he told Xiaogouzi.

Xiaogouzi mumbled without agreeing or refusing. This move was utterly unexpected. A countryman felt apprehensive at the mere mention of the county yamen. Its clerks brought to mind the fierce-faced judges in the City God's temple. If a clerk in the revenue office said, “We must go out to the village and investigate first,” the whole fraud would be exposed. Yet the procedure was perfectly proper, and Xiaogouzi could think of no excuse to refuse. His face reddened with anxiety. Then, seeing Zhou's knowing smile and the documents clenched in his hand, he suddenly understood. Before any silver had reached him, the others had secured evidence against him. He was in for a terrible fall. The thought struck like a blow on the head, sending stars before his eyes. In his panic he lost all sense of tactics and reached for the papers. He failed to seize them, but Zhou broke into a sweat, hastily thrust them inside his clothing, jumped back two paces and pressed both hands over his chest. “Hey! What are you doing?” Realizing that he had virtually exposed himself, Xiaogouzi turned ashen. He pointed at Zhou in agitation. “This is too much trouble! I won't concern myself with it any more. Take out the papers and tear them up. Let it be as though none of this happened.” Zhou was quick enough to see that he should now play the angry accuser, leaving Hu to intervene and negotiate. He raised a hand to rebuff Xiaogouzi, put on a fierce expression and said, “Wait. Let's make this clear. What exactly are you up to? I've treated you as a friend with all sincerity. Don't behave like a fool and leave me unable to account for myself to Mr Hu.” “No, no, that's not it!” Xiaogouzi protested vehemently. “I meant well too, but this really is a troublesome business to meddle in. Brother Zhou, do me a kindness and return the papers.” “Return them?” Zhou's expression changed, and he gave a cold laugh. “Do you think it's that easy?”

Xiaogouzi stared at him wide-eyed, without blinking, as though he had never truly seen his face before. Hu understood his feelings. Zhou still lacked finesse; he should not have turned hostile so abruptly. Hu hurried to intervene. “Let's talk calmly. Something written in black and white can't simply be torn up. Tell us what makes this so ‘troublesome’. Explain your difficulty, and we can discuss it.” Xiaogouzi's difficulty was precisely that he could not explain it. In desperation he seized upon someone else as a shield. Pointing at Chen, he said, “He's an honest fellow who's never been inside a yamen. He certainly won't agree to register the papers at the revenue office. Doesn't that put us intermediaries in a difficult position? Luckily, no money has changed hands. Let's cancel everything. Here's the husband; you can discuss it face to face and begin again. If you reach agreement, I'll be there to act as intermediary. If you don't, I've merely made a journey and run an errand for nothing.” His argument twisted reason, but he managed quite a speech. Hu smiled. “We've already agreed and drawn up the papers. What is there left to discuss? If he doesn't wish to go to the yamen, never mind. It'll only take a little more trouble. We'll all go by boat to Mudu and ask your Chen clan head to witness the matter. Surely that will do?” The fraud would still be exposed, but at least not until they reached Mudu. Xiaogouzi thought he could gain a little breathing space. He braced himself and answered, “Very well.” “Then when do we leave?” “Whenever you like. We can go at once.”

Xiaogouzi sounded resolute, but the other honest fellow lacked even his small skill in pretence. Chen could no longer keep calm. He tugged at Xiaogouzi's clothes and whispered, “We can't go.” “What do you mean, we can't?” Xiaogouzi snapped. “What are you afraid of?” “Yes, what?” Zhou added coldly. “The worst that can happen is a lawsuit.” This made Chen more anxious still. Having already told Hu the truth, how could he continue muddling along with Xiaogouzi? Yet he could hardly say openly that their host knew of the impersonation and no amount of bold talk would help. He merely wrung his hands. “Let's talk it over a little more.” Hu saw his distress and seized upon the opening. “Then let's talk. The matter must reach a satisfactory conclusion. Go and discuss it among yourselves.” This temporarily eased the strain. Xiaogouzi and his companions withdrew to confer in whispers. Hu and Zhou exchanged a smile and likewise sought a quiet place to assess the situation and decide their next move.

“He is an impostor, just as we thought.” Hu told Zhou what Chen had said, then frowned. “I'm afraid this will mean more trouble for you.” “Gladly!” After two days of unfailing success in Hu's service, Zhou's confidence had grown considerably. Eager for action, he declared, “I'll go myself and see it through, whatever it takes.” “Don't assume it'll be easy...” In Hu's analysis, Xiaogouzi must have found the proper course blocked, yet could not bear to give up that pile of gleaming ingots. He had therefore risked this inferior scheme in the hope of getting lucky. If that was right, there must be some obstacle on A’qiao's husband's side. They must first discover it before acting. “Easy enough,” Zhou said. “I'll put pressure on Xiaogouzi. We have evidence against him. He won't dare withhold the truth.” Once the truth was forced out, it proved that Hu had misjudged the matter this time. Xiaogouzi, who followed no honest occupation, had intended to obtain the money by fraud and disappear. A’qiao's husband knew nothing of the affair. Of course, Zhou elicited these facts through indirect questioning. Xiaogouzi proposed that they wipe the slate clean. He would accompany Hu to Mudu, bring the parties together and reopen negotiations. He promised not to manipulate matters or inflate the price for his own profit. His only hope was that, if an agreement was reached and put in writing, he might still earn an intermediary's fee. Hu accepted. Generously, he destroyed the document then and there, appointed Zhou as his representative, and sent him off to Mudu at once.
